objective_for_doctor: Evaluate and diagnose the patient presenting with shortness of breath, increased abdominal girth, and a large ovarian mass.

turns.content: Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—first, how old are you, and how long have you been short of breath and noticed increasing abdominal size? Doctor: Any known ovarian cyst/tumor history, and have you had pelvic pain, early satiety, nausea/vomiting, or abnormal vaginal bleeding? Doctor: I’ll listen to your lungs and check your abdomen for ascites/tense distension—any fever, chest pain, leg swelling, or weight loss?

Patient: I’m 40, and my shortness of breath and increasing abdominal size have been going on for about a month. I don’t have any known history of ovarian cysts or tumors, and I haven’t had pelvic pain, early satiety, nausea/vomiting, or abnormal vaginal bleeding. I’ve also not had fever, chest pain, leg swelling, or significant weight loss.

Doctor: On exam, I’m checking for ascites—does your abdomen feel very bloated/“full of fluid,” and have you noticed any reduced urine output or sudden worsening breathing when lying flat? Doctor: Also, any family history of ovarian/breast cancer, and have you had recent pregnancy, missed periods, or use of fertility drugs or hormonal therapy?

Patient: My abdomen feels steadily bloated and “full,” but I haven’t noticed reduced urine output, and my breathing doesn’t suddenly get worse when I lie flat. I don’t have a known family history of ovarian or breast cancer, and I’m not recently pregnant, not missing periods, and I haven’t used fertility drugs or hormonal therapy.

Doctor: I’m going to examine your abdomen for shifting dullness/fluid wave and I’ll order key labs and imaging—REQUEST TEST: Pelvic_Abdominal_Ultrasound (with Doppler) and REQUEST TEST: Serum_Cancer_Markers (CA-125, CEA, AFP ± β-hCG). Doctor: Also, to see if this is malignant ascites or another cardiopulmonary cause, REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_Abdomen_Pelvis with contrast and REQUEST TEST: CBC_CMP_Coagulation_profile.

RESULTS: Temperature 36.8°C (98°F); BP 125/80 mmHg; HR 85 bpm; RR 20 breaths/min. CBC: WBC 8,500 /μL; Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL; Platelets 275,000 /μL. Respiratory exam: mild accessory muscle use; dullness right lower lung fields; decreased breath sounds right basal areas. Chest X-ray: right-sided pleural effusion. Abdominal exam: visible distension; normal bowel sounds; shifting dullness/positive fluid wave suggestive of ascites; non-tender. Pelvic exam: palpable right pelvic mass. Abdominal ultrasound: large right ovarian mass with significant ascites. CA-125: normal. Doctor: Thank you—given a large right ovarian mass with clear ascites on ultrasound, plus a right pleural effusion and normal CA-125, the leading concern is an ovarian tumor with Meigs-/pseudo-Meigs–type presentation (malignant effusion/ascites) versus a benign fibroma/thecoma variant; my next step is to confirm via CT findings and tumor markers. Doctor: REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_Abdomen_Pelvis_with_contrast (to assess omental/peritoneal disease and pleural/lymph spread) and REQUEST TEST: CEA_plus_AFP_plus_β-hCG (± repeat CA-125) plus REQUEST TEST: Pelvic_Abdominal_Ultrasound_with_Doppler (tumor vascularity). Doctor: If imaging shows no widespread metastases and there’s resolution of effusions after tumor removal, that would strongly support Meigs syndrome (classically ovarian fibroma); otherwise we’d treat as ovarian malignancy causing ascites/pleural effusion. Doctor: DIAGNOSIS READY: Ovarian tumor presenting with ascites and right pleural effusion—most consistent with Meigs/pseudo-Meigs syndrome pending CT and definitive pathology.
